label: SCDES AI Governance Framework
heading: Purpose
text:
Purpose
The South Carolina Department of Environmental Services Enterprise Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework (framework) is established for the evaluation, approval, deployment, and ongoing oversight of artificial intelligence systems within the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services (Agency). Its adoption reflects a determination by Agency leadership that AI presents both meaningful opportunity and material risk for a state environmental regulatory agency. As of the date of adoption, artificial intelligence is a nascent and emerging technology, one which is only beginning to enter operational deployment in governmental settings. This framework and associated policies and procedures have been created in an attempt to support the ethical, responsible, and efficient deployment of this technology for our employees and the citizens we serve. The goal of this framework is to create standards which help our Agency, and the public feel confident that we are putting our best faith efforts into this endeavor and to serve as a model to others.
This framework is SCDES’s agency-level implementation of the South Carolina State Agencies Artificial Intelligence Strategy, published in June 2024 by the South Carolina Department of Administration. The State Agency AI Strategy outlines five guiding principles for AI adoption by a state agency. SCDES intends to comply with these guiding principles by developing AI technologies: Safely and Securely, Fairly and Objectively, Ethically, Transparently, and Beneficially. This framework is also designed to comply with applicable federal requirements, including Office of Management and Budget Memorandum M-25-21 and the National Institute of Standards and Technology AI Risk Management Framework as of the date of adoption. Where this framework imposes requirements more stringent than state or federal policy, the more stringent standard controls.
Procedural detail implementing this framework is set forth in the SCDES AI Operations Manual. Where this framework states a rule, the Operations Manual states how the rule is carried out. The Operations Manual is owned by the AI Governance Council and may be updated to reflect operational experience without amendment of this framework, provided that the Operations Manual remains consistent with the rules established in this framework.

label: SCDES AI Governance Framework
heading: Scope
text:
Scope
This framework applies to all programs, bureaus, and offices within SCDES. Its requirements attach to any AI system developed internally by Agency staff, procured from external vendors, embedded within third-party platforms, or acquired through cooperative purchasing agreements, multi-state contracts, or platform upgrades. The framework governs AI systems at every lifecycle stage, from conceptual evaluation through retirement, and applies to any system employing machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, or generative AI techniques, regardless of whether the AI capability is the primary function of the platform. The scope applies to future-developed technology not yet conceived.
Three categories of technology are expressly excluded: conventional statistical analysis that does not employ machine learning techniques (such as traditional statistical analysis system (SAS) software); deterministic automation that follows fixed, predefined rules without adaptive learning (such as form-based workflows); and routine data analytics tools that aggregate or visualize data without predictive or generative capabilities (such as Power BI). Where uncertainty exists as to whether a particular tool falls within or outside this framework's scope, the Chief Technology Officer (CTO) shall make the determination, subject to AI Governance Council’s review.

label: SCDES AI Governance Framework
heading: Definitions
text:
Definitions
The following terms carry specific meaning throughout this framework and the Operations Manual. Where a term is used in a manner that departs from common usage, the definition below controls.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to any system that performs tasks typically requiring human judgment, pattern recognition, or predictive analysis, including machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative AI, regardless of vendor label.
AI System means any software tool employing AI techniques, whether standalone or integrated into a larger platform, including platforms where the AI function is ancillary to the platform's primary purpose.
AI Registry is the centralized inventory of all AI systems in use, under evaluation, in pilot, or retired within the Agency, as established by Section 7A.
Algorithmic Bias means systematic and unfair discrimination in AI outputs resulting from deficiencies in training data, model design, or deployment context, which may manifest as negative impacts on protected populations absent discriminatory intent.
Autonomous Decision System is an AI tool that executes actions or generates outputs without intervening human review. No autonomous decision system is authorized under this framework. Any AI system discovered operating autonomously without express authorization shall be immediately suspended and treated as a Level 3 incident under Section 11.
Decision-Support System is an AI tool that provides analysis, recommendations, or risk scores to inform human decisions without replacing them. This is the only category of AI-influenced decision-making currently authorized under this framework. AI-powered assistive tools, including productivity assistants and workflow automation bots, are decision-support systems provided no Agency action is finalized without human review.
Delegated Federal Program means a federal program in which SCDES has a formal agreement with the federal agency to implement the program in lieu of federal implementation. This framework applies to AI use in all programs delegated to SCDES by USEPA, USFDA, USNRC, NOAA, or any other federal agency.
Information Retrieval Tools are content- and context-restrained AI systems such as chatbots, virtual assistants, and AI-enabled search interfaces. They are classified as decision-support systems, provided they do not finalize Agency action, the underlying content has been reviewed by qualified Agency personnel, the tool discloses its AI nature to users, and the tool provides a clear path to a qualified human.
Model Drift refers to the degradation of an AI model's performance over time due to changes in input data, regulatory requirements, or environmental conditions. Monitoring procedures are set forth in the Operations Manual.
Shadow AI means the unauthorized or unregistered use of AI tools by Agency personnel outside this framework. Shadow AI is prohibited.
Synthetic Data means data artificially generated by an algorithm, statistical model, or generative AI system rather than collected from real-world observations. Synthetic data shall not be used as the basis for any regulatory determination, enforcement action, permitting decision, or official Department finding. Disclosure obligations are set forth in the Operations Manual.
Vendor-Embedded AI refers to AI capabilities integrated into third-party software platforms used by the Agency. Vendor-embedded AI is subject to Section 8A.

label: SCDES AI Governance Framework
heading: Operating Principles
text:
Operating Principles
All AI activity within SCDES shall adhere to the following binding principles. Where a proposed deployment cannot satisfy one or more of them, the proposal shall not proceed unless the AI Governance Council grants a documented exception with conditions, a remediation timeline, or explicit acceptance of the documented risks.
Accessibility. AI systems and their outputs shall be accessible to persons with disabilities in compliance with Title II of the ADA, Section 504 and Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act, and later adopted rules or regulations regarding accessibility. No AI deployment shall create a barrier to the public participating in or accessing government services.
Continuity. Every AI deployment shall be accompanied by documented manual fallback procedures. No AI deployment may create a dependency that the Agency cannot exit.
Data Security and Cybersecurity. AI systems are subject to the Agency's existing information security, cybersecurity, data privacy, and acceptable use requirements without modification. The substantive security determination rests within the Office of the CTO under the authority of the Chief Information Security and Data Officer (CISDO).
Data Stewardship. The State of South Carolina retains control of its data at all times. No vendor, contractor, or AI system may use, retain, or repurpose state data inconsistently with Sections 8 and 8A.
Fiscal Responsibility. The full lifecycle cost of any AI deployment shall be understood and documented before commitment, and actual costs shall be tracked against projections.
Human Accountability. Final decision authority for all regulatory determinations, enforcement actions, and public-facing services rests with qualified Agency personnel. AI may inform, accelerate, or augment human judgment, but it may not supplant it.
Interoperability. AI systems should use open standards where practicable and avoid proprietary architectures that constrain the Agency's future flexibility.
Measurable Value. AI systems shall produce outcomes quantifiable against documented baseline data. Systems that cannot demonstrate measurable value at annual review are subject to suspension or sunset.
Mission Alignment. AI shall demonstrably advance the Agency's statutory responsibilities, service delivery, or public benefit. AI adopted without a clear nexus to mission outcomes is not authorized.
Non-Discrimination. AI systems shall operate in a manner consistent with applicable federal and state non-discrimination laws.
Risk Management. No AI deployment shall create unacceptable environmental, legal, or operational risk. Risk is classified under Section 7, and oversight intensity is graduated accordingly.
Transparency. AI use shall be explainable to oversight bodies, the regulated community, and the public, in non-technical terms covering what each AI system does, what data it uses, how its outputs influence Agency decisions, and what safeguards are in place.
